items.title: Rise of the Guptas — On the Ruins of the Kushanas
items.body:
## A New North Indian Empire

- On the ruins of the **Kushana** empire (north) and the **Satavahana** empire (Deccan) arose the empire of the **Guptas**.
- Though **not as large as the Mauryas**, it kept **North India politically united** for over a century — roughly **A.D. 240 to 550**.
- The Guptas were originally **feudatories of the Kushanas** and set up powerful monarchs first controlling the **Magadha region of Bihar**, later expanding to **UP** and former Kushana/Satavahana lands.
- Their strength rested on **iron-ore reserves of central India and south Bihar** and on **proximity to the silk trade** with the **Byzantine empire**.
- They **patronised poets, musicians and scholars** (e.g. Kalidasa, Shudraka, Varahamihira), and the age saw the flowering of **Indian science**.
keyPoints: Guptas rose on the ruins of the Kushanas (north) and Satavahanas (Deccan).
Kept North India united c. A.D. 240–550, though smaller than the Mauryan empire.
Originally feudatories of the Kushanas; base in Magadha (Bihar), later UP.
Wealth from central India/south Bihar iron ore and Byzantine silk trade.
Great patrons of poets, musicians and science — Kalidasa, Shudraka, Varahamihira.
items.mnemonic: Guptas = '240 to 550', from Magadha iron & Byzantine silk.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (overview; The situation around 300 AD; Gupta Kings Overview)

items.title: The Gupta Rulers — Order & Timeline
items.body:
## Succession of the Guptas

- **Sri Gupta** (c. 240–280 CE) — founder, title *Maharaja*.
- **Ghatotkacha** (280–319 CE) — his son, title *Maharaja*.
- **Chandragupta I** (319–335 CE) — first true emperor, *Maharajadhiraja*; Lichchhavi alliance.
- **Samudragupta** (335–380 CE) — the great conqueror, *Kaviraja*; Prayag Prashasti.
- **Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya'** (380–413/415 CE) — defeated the Shakas; Navaratnas.
- **Kumaragupta I** (415–455 CE) — *Mahendraditya*; founded Nalanda University.
- **Skandagupta** (455–467 CE) — repaired Sudarshan Lake; resisted the Hunas.
- Later weak rulers — Purugupta, Kumaragupta II, Buddhagupta, Narasimhagupta, Kumaragupta III, and **Vishnugupta** (last ruler, c. 540–550 CE).
keyPoints: Sri Gupta → Ghatotkacha → Chandragupta I → Samudragupta → Chandragupta II.
Chandragupta II followed by Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta (the great line).
Chandragupta I was the first to take Maharajadhiraja; Sri Gupta/Ghatotkacha were 'Maharaja'.
Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda; Skandagupta fought the earliest Huna invasions.
Vishnugupta (c. 540–550 CE) was the last known Gupta ruler.
items.mnemonic: Rulers in order: 'Sri Ghost Chandra Samudra Chandra Kumar Skanda' — Sri Gupta, Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta, Skandagupta.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Gupta Kings Overview table)

items.title: Sri Gupta & Ghatotkacha — The Founders
items.body:
## Laying the Foundation

- **Sri Gupta (c. 240–280 CE)** was the **founder of the Gupta dynasty** and used the title **'Maharaja'**.
- The **Poona copper-plate inscription of Prabhavatigupta** (daughter of Chandragupta II) describes Sri Gupta as the **'Adhiraja'** of the Gupta dynasty.
- During his reign, **northern or central Bengal** may have been the home of the Guptas.
- **Ghatotkacha (280–319 CE)**, the **son of Sri Gupta**, also bore the title **'Maharaja'**; his was a **peaceful period** for the young dynasty.
keyPoints: Sri Gupta (c. 240–280 CE) founded the dynasty; title 'Maharaja'.
Poona copper inscription of Prabhavatigupta calls Sri Gupta the 'Adhiraja'.
The Guptas' home may have been in north/central Bengal under Sri Gupta.
Ghatotkacha (280–319 CE), son of Sri Gupta, also used 'Maharaja'.
Ghatotkacha's reign was a peaceful, consolidating period.
items.mnemonic: Founders were mere 'Maharajas'; the Poona plate of Prabhavatigupta names Sri Gupta 'Adhiraja'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Sri Gupta; Ghatotkach)

items.title: Chandragupta I — Lichchhavi Alliance & First Emperor
items.body:
## The First Gupta Emperor (319–335 CE)

- **Chandragupta I**, son of Ghatotkacha, was the **first true emperor** of the dynasty and took the grand title **Maharajadhiraja** ('great king of kings').
- He forged a **matrimonial alliance** by marrying the **Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi** — the Lichchhavis were an ancient clan headquartered at **Vaishali (Bihar)**.
- This alliance boosted Gupta prestige; he ruled around **Ayodhya, Prayaga and Magadha**, expanding the kingdom from the **Ganges to Prayag**.
- Under him the Guptas **issued gold coins in large quantities**, including the famous **King-and-Queen (Kumaradevi) type** commemorating the Lichchhavi marriage.
keyPoints: Chandragupta I (319–335 CE) = first true Gupta emperor; title Maharajadhiraja.
Married Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi (Lichchhavis based at Vaishali, Bihar).
Ruled Ayodhya, Prayaga and Magadha; expanded from the Ganges to Prayag.
Issued gold coins in large quantities.
Kumaradevi (King-and-Queen) coins commemorate the Lichchhavi alliance.
items.mnemonic: Chandragupta I = 'Maharajadhiraja' + married Lichchhavi Kumaradevi = King-Queen coins.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta-I; Numismatic art)

items.title: Samudragupta — 'Napoleon of India' & the Prayag Prashasti
items.body:
## The Great Conqueror (335–380 CE)

- **Samudragupta**, son of Chandragupta I, was called the **'Napoleon of India'** by historians for his conquests; he pursued a **policy of blood and iron**.
- The **Allahabad (Prayag) Pillar inscription** — a **prashasti (eulogy) composed by his courtier Harishena** — records his extensive campaigns: he defeated **four kings of North India** and warred across **Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu**.
- He received **tribute from Assam, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia**.
- Bearing the title **Kaviraja ('King of Poets')**, he was a gifted **poet and musician** — his gold coins famously show him **playing the veena**.
- He performed the **Ashvamedha (horse) sacrifice** to proclaim imperial sovereignty and, per his coins, **remained undefeated**.

figure.alt: Gupta gold dinar showing a seated Gupta king, of the type issued by Samudragupta
figure.caption: Gupta gold dinar of the Samudragupta type — his coins depict the emperor as both warrior and veena-playing musician-poet (Kaviraja).

keyPoints: Samudragupta (335–380 CE) = 'Napoleon of India'; policy of blood and iron.
Allahabad/Prayag Prashasti composed by his courtier Harishena details his conquests.
Campaigned across N. India, Odisha, Andhra and Tamil Nadu; tribute from Assam, Sri Lanka, SE Asia.
Title Kaviraja ('King of Poets'); coins show him playing the veena.
Performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and claimed to remain undefeated.
items.mnemonic: Samudragupta = 'Napoleon of India'; Prayag Prashasti by Harishena; veena on his coins.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Samudragupta; Allahabad pillar; Numismatic art)

items.title: Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' — Shakas Defeated & Fa-Hien
items.body:
## Vikramaditya (380–413/415 CE)

- **Chandragupta II**, son of Samudragupta, also styled **Vikramaditya** (and *Simhavikrama*), continued his father's expansionist policy.
- He **defeated the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas)**, conquering **Malwa and Gujarat**, and extended the empire from the **Indus in the west to Bengal in the east**, and from the **Himalayan foothills to the Narmada**.
- His daughter **Prabhavatigupta** became a **queen of the southern Vakataka kingdom**, extending Gupta influence into the Deccan.
- The **Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien** visited India **during his reign** and described a **peaceful and prosperous kingdom**.
- He was a great **patron of learning and the arts**, famously maintaining the **Navaratnas (Nine Gems)**.

figure.alt: Map of Asian trade routes c. A.D. 400 showing the extent of the Gupta Empire from the Indus to Bengal
figure.caption: The Gupta Empire c. A.D. 400 under Chandragupta II — stretching from the Indus to Bengal and linked to Asian trade routes carrying cloth, ivory, spices and gold.

keyPoints: Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' (380–413/415 CE), son of Samudragupta.
Defeated the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas); won Malwa and Gujarat.
Empire from the Indus to Bengal, Himalayan foothills to the Narmada.
Daughter Prabhavatigupta was a Vakataka queen (Deccan influence).
Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited during his reign; patron of the Navaratnas.
items.mnemonic: Chandragupta II = Vikramaditya: 'Vanquished Shakas, Visited by Fa-Hien, kept the Nine Gems'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta-II; Fa-Hien)

items.title: The Navaratnas & Kalidasa
items.body:
## Nine Gems of Vikramaditya's Court

- **Chandragupta II Vikramaditya** patronised the **Navaratnas (Nine Gems)**, a galaxy of scholars that made his court a byword for learning.
- The greatest was **Kalidasa** (4th–5th century), author of **Raghuvansham, Kumarasambhava, Abhijnana Shakuntalam** and **Meghdoot** — the finest classical Sanskrit poet-dramatist.
- **Vishakhadatta** wrote the political drama **Mudrarakshasa**; **Shudraka** wrote **Mrichchhakatika** ('The Little Clay Cart').
- **Amarasimha**, a luminary of Chandragupta II's court, compiled the **Amarakosha** (Sanskrit lexicon).
- The court's brilliance made the Gupta age the **classical golden age of Sanskrit literature**.
keyPoints: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya patronised the Navaratnas (Nine Gems).
Kalidasa: Raghuvansham, Kumarasambhava, Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Meghdoot.
Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa; Shudraka wrote Mrichchhakatika.
Amarasimha (court luminary) compiled the Amarakosha.
The Gupta court was the classical golden age of Sanskrit literature.
items.mnemonic: Navaratnas' star = Kalidasa: 'RaKuAM' — Raghuvansham, Kumarasambhava, Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Meghdoot.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Chandragupta-II; Literature table — Kalidasa, Vishakhadatta, Shudrak; Amarakosha)

items.title: The Mehrauli Iron Pillar
items.body:
## Testament to Gupta Metallurgy

- The **Mehrauli Iron Pillar** was made during the **Gupta period** and later **moved to Delhi by Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.
- It carries **inscriptions of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)** recounting the **conquests and achievements** of the king.
- Its **rust-resistant iron** is celebrated as evidence of the **advanced metallurgy** of Gupta India.
- Alongside the **Allahabad (Prayag) pillar** of Samudragupta, it represents the era's outstanding **pillar art**.
keyPoints: Mehrauli Iron Pillar was made in the Gupta period.
Later moved to Delhi by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
Bears inscriptions of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) on his conquests.
Its rust-resistance shows advanced Gupta metallurgy.
With Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar, a highlight of Gupta pillar art.
items.mnemonic: Mehrauli Iron Pillar = Chandragupta II's rust-proof column, later shifted to Delhi by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Pillar art; The Mehrauli Iron Pillar)

items.title: Kumaragupta I — Founder of Nalanda University
items.body:
## Kumaragupta I (415–455 CE)

- **Kumaragupta I**, son of Chandragupta II, bore the titles **Shakraditya** and **Mahendraditya**.
- He was **instrumental in establishing Nalanda University**, the great Buddhist centre of learning.
- He is famous for the **Bhitari pillar inscription** (near Gorakhpur) and for **proliferating gold coins**.
- He performed the **Ashvamedha sacrifice** to assert imperial sovereignty, though there is **no concrete evidence of major military conquests** in his reign.
keyPoints: Kumaragupta I (415–455 CE); titles Shakraditya and Mahendraditya.
Instrumental in founding Nalanda University.
Famous for the Bhitari pillar inscription near Gorakhpur.
Issued abundant gold coins; performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice.
No concrete evidence of major military achievements.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Kumara Gupta; Nalanda University)

items.title: Gupta Administration — Bhuktis, Vishayas & Shrenis
items.body:
## Provincial & Local Government

- Important cities were **Pataliputra, Prayag and Ujjain**; **salaries were paid in cash for the first time**, later replaced by a **land-revenue system**.
- The centralising Mauryan tendency **declined** amid an emerging **feudal system**, so **governors played a major role**.
- Administrative hierarchy:
  - **Bhuktis** — the largest units (provinces), under **Uparikas**.
  - **Vishayas** — districts, under **Vishayapati**.
  - **Vithis** — (in eastern India) sub-districts, further divided into **villages**, where **village headmen** grew important.
- **Shrenis** were **guilds of artisans and merchants** governed by their own laws; seals from **Vaishali and Bhita** show they flourished, and the **ivory-carvers' guild of Vidisha** funded the **southern gateway of the Sanchi stupa**.
keyPoints: Key cities: Pataliputra, Prayag, Ujjain; cash salaries first, later land revenue.
Feudal tendencies rose; provincial governors grew powerful.
Bhuktis (provinces, under Uparikas) → Vishayas (districts, under Vishayapati) → Vithis → villages.
Village headmen became important in local administration.
Shrenis (guilds) self-governed; Vidisha ivory-carvers funded Sanchi's southern gateway.
items.mnemonic: Admin ladder: 'Bhukti → Vishaya → Vithi → Village' (Uparika, then Vishayapati).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Gupta Administration; Bhuktis; Visayas; Vithis; Shrenis)

items.title: Golden Age — Science: Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Zero & Decimals
items.body:
## Scientific Efflorescence

- The Gupta age (c. 240–550 AD) is the **'Golden Age of India'**, marked by advances in science, mathematics, astronomy and the arts.
- **Aryabhata** proposed, for the first time, that the **earth revolves around the Sun**; he is credited with the concept of **zero** and the **decimal system** in mathematics.
- **Varahamihira** made great contributions to astronomy/astrology; his **Panchasiddhantika (505 AD)** summarised five earlier siddhantas — **Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha and Paitamaha**.
- The **Romaka Siddhanta** name betrays **Greek (Roman) influence** on Indian astronomy of the period.
keyPoints: Gupta age = the 'Golden Age of India' (c. 240–550 AD).
Aryabhata: earth revolves around the Sun; concept of zero and the decimal system.
Varahamihira: Panchasiddhantika (505 AD), summarising five siddhantas.
The five siddhantas: Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha, Paitamaha.
Romaka Siddhanta shows Greek/Roman influence on Indian astronomy.
items.mnemonic: Aryabhata gave 'Zero, Decimals & heliocentric Sun'; Varahamihira wrote Pancha-siddhantika (505).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Golden age; Science and Technology — Aryabhatt; Varahamihira)

items.title: Golden Age — Art, Temples & the Sultanganj Buddha
items.body:
## Art & Temple Architecture

- The Gupta period was a **golden age of architecture**. The finest cave art is at **Ajanta and Ellora**, with celebrated **mural paintings** (Ajanta on Buddhist themes; Ellora on Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical themes).
- The **Sultanganj Buddha** — a **7.5-ft** figure of **cream-coloured sandstone using metal** — is a masterpiece of the age (Gupta–Pala transitional sculpture).
- The Gupta period marked the **beginning of temple architecture**; three styles emerged: the **Nagara** school (North India — e.g. **Dashavatara temple, Deogarh**), the **Dravidian** school (South India), and the later **Vesara** school (a blend).
- Secular Sanskrit literature also flourished, with **Bhasa's thirteen plays** and the revival of the **Puranas**.

figure.alt: Bronze standing Buddha of the Gupta period (Sultanganj-type) with clinging drapery
figure.caption: A Gupta-era standing Buddha (Sultanganj type) — the classical Gupta idiom of serene features and clinging, near-transparent drapery.

keyPoints: Ajanta & Ellora caves — finest Gupta-age murals (Buddhist / also Jain & Brahmanical at Ellora).
Sultanganj Buddha: 7.5 ft, cream sandstone using metal (Gupta–Pala transitional).
Gupta period began temple architecture.
Styles: Nagara (Dashavatara temple, Deogarh), Dravidian, and later Vesara.
Secular literature flourished — Bhasa's 13 plays; Puranas revived.
items.mnemonic: Gupta art: Ajanta–Ellora caves, Sultanganj Buddha, and the first Nagara temple (Deogarh).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Architecture — Caves, Sculptures, Temple architecture; Literature)

items.title: Nalanda University & Fa-Hien's Account
items.body:
## Education & the Society Fa-Hien Saw

- **Nalanda University** emerged under **Kumaragupta's rule (415–455 AD)** and later flourished under **Harshavardhana** and the **Pala kings**.
- Its teaching centred on **Mahayana Buddhism**, alongside the **Vedas, fine arts, grammar, philosophy, logic and medicine**; it deeply influenced **Tibetan Buddhism**.
- The Chinese pilgrim **Fa-Hien (399 AD)** travelled via China–Gobi–Central Asia to India; he recorded that religions **lived in peace**, people were **law-abiding and vegetarian**, punishments were **not severe**, and there was **no spy system**.
- He also **visited Nalanda**, noting its exams, teachers, scholars and books.
keyPoints: Nalanda University emerged under Kumaragupta I (415–455 AD).
Flourished later under Harshavardhana and the Pala kings.
Taught Mahayana Buddhism plus Vedas, grammar, logic, philosophy, medicine.
Fa-Hien (399 AD) reached India via China–Gobi–Central Asia.
Fa-Hien described a peaceful, law-abiding, vegetarian society with no spy system.
items.mnemonic: Nalanda = Kumaragupta's foundation; Fa-Hien (399 AD) saw a peaceful, vegetarian, spy-free society.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Fa-Hien; Nalanda University; Society During the Gupta Age)

items.title: Gupta Coinage — Gold Dinaras
items.body:
## The Golden Numismatics

- The Gupta Empire issued **large-scale gold coins called 'Dinaras'**, a hallmark of its prosperity.
- **Chandragupta I** issued the **Kumaradevi (King-and-Queen) type**, showing the king and his Lichchhavi wife.
- **Samudragupta's** coins famously depict him **playing the veena**, reflecting his fame as a poet-musician.
- Other coin motifs include the **reclining Lion** and the **Ashvamedha (horse-sacrifice)** type.
- Abundant gold coinage financed **trade** and reflected surplus wealth in the age.

figure.alt: Gupta gold dinar depicting a seated Gupta emperor
figure.caption: A Gupta gold dinar — the Guptas' abundant gold coinage (dinaras) is a hallmark of the age's prosperity.

keyPoints: Guptas issued large-scale gold coins called 'Dinaras'.
Chandragupta I: Kumaradevi (King-and-Queen) type coins.
Samudragupta: coins showing him playing the veena.
Other types: reclining Lion and Ashvamedha (horse-sacrifice).
Gold coinage fuelled trade and reflected surplus wealth.
items.mnemonic: Gupta gold = 'Dinaras': Kumaradevi (king-queen), Veena (Samudragupta), Lion & Ashvamedha.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Numismatic art)

items.title: Decline of the Guptas — Huna Invasions & Skandagupta
items.body:
## Why the Empire Fell

- **Later rulers were too weak** to hold the empire, and **governors became powerful**, behaving like independent rulers under the growing **feudal/land-revenue system**.
- **Huna (Hun) invasions** from the **north-west frontier** severely weakened the Guptas.
- **Skandagupta (455–467 CE)**, son of Kumaragupta, **fought bravely against the earliest Huna invasions** and also **repaired the Sudarshan Lake** — but his successors could not check the Hunas.
- By the mid-5th century large parts of **western and northern India** fell to the Hunas.
- Successor states arose — **Pushyabhutis at Thanesar, Pratiharas at Kannauj, Chauhans in Rajasthan, Palas near Odisha**, and others — as the empire disintegrated by c. 550 CE.
keyPoints: Weak later rulers and over-mighty provincial governors weakened the empire.
Huna (Hun) invasions from the north-west were a major cause of decline.
Skandagupta (455–467 CE) fought the earliest Hunas and repaired Sudarshan Lake.
His successors could not check the Hunas; W & N India fell by mid-5th century.
Successor states: Pushyabhutis (Thanesar), Pratiharas (Kannauj), Chauhans, Palas, etc.
items.mnemonic: Gupta decline = 'Weak kings + strong governors + Hunas'; Skandagupta was the last great defender.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Gupta Empire (Skandagupta; Decline of the Gupta Empire)

items.title: Author–Work Pairs the PYQs Hinge On
items.body:
## Gupta-Age Author → Work (UPSC author:work pairs)

| Author | Work(s) |
|---|---|
| **Kalidasa** | Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Meghaduta, Ritusamhara, Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam |
| **Vishakhadatta** | **Mudrarakshasa** and **Devichandraguptam** (both political dramas) |
| **Shudraka** | Mrichchhakatika ('The Little Clay Cart') |
| **Amarasimha** | Amarakosha (Sanskrit lexicon) |
| **Aryabhata** | Aryabhatiya |
| **Varahamihira** | **Panchasiddhantika** (astronomy) and **Brihat Samhita** (encyclopaedic) and Brihat Jataka |
| **Vatsyayana** | Nyaya Bhashya (and, earlier, the Kamasutra) |

- The exam trap: **Vishakhadatta wrote BOTH Mudrarakshasa AND Devichandraguptam** — the latter dramatizes a Gupta succession episode.
- **Varahamihira** is tested via **Brihat Samhita** (a wide-ranging treatise on astronomy, astrology, architecture, gemmology) as often as via the Panchasiddhantika.
keyPoints: Vishakhadatta wrote both the Mudrarakshasa and the Devichandraguptam.
Shudraka wrote the Mrichchhakatika; Amarasimha compiled the Amarakosha.
Varahamihira wrote the Panchasiddhantika AND the Brihat Samhita (and Brihat Jataka).
Aryabhata's work is the Aryabhatiya.
Kalidasa's dramas: Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam; epics Raghuvamsha & Kumarasambhava.
items.source: standard NCERT/Britannica facts on Gupta-age authors and works
